name: Wheat Belly diet

lead: The Wheat Belly diet comes from cardiologist William Davis's 2011 book. It asks followers to remove wheat and other grains, and the claimed appearance payoff is a smaller waist and less abdominal fat.
Supporters report weight loss and a flatter stomach. Critics in nutrition science say the book's claims are not supported by published studies, and dietitians count it among fad diets.

paras: Followers cut out wheat and grains and follow a low-carbohydrate pattern, replacing them with other foods such as vegetables, nuts and seeds. Davis says a healthy plant-based version is possible without grains.
Dietitians note that restricting grains may lower intake of B vitamins, calcium and vitamin D. Gluten itself has documented adverse effects for people with coeliac disease and related conditions.

angle.text: Followers use grain avoidance as a route to fat loss around the waist. Claimed results come mainly from the book's author and testimonials.

lead: The Wheat Belly diet is a wheat-avoidance eating plan from American cardiologist William Davis, whose book Wheat Belly was published in 2011 and became a New York Times bestseller.[1] Davis argues that modern wheat drives overeating and weight gain, and followers use the plan to reduce belly fat and body weight, which changes how the midsection looks.[1]

Reviewers have been critical. A 2013 review in the Journal of Cereal Science concluded the book's statements could not be supported by published studies, and the American Association of Cereal Chemists noted most studies found no link between refined grains and weight gain or chronic disease, according to the encyclopedia account.[1] Dietitians cite the plan as a fad diet and note possible gaps in B vitamins, calcium and vitamin D.[1]
Separately, medical literature documents adverse effects of wheat gluten in conditions such as coeliac disease.[2]

paras: Davis calls modern wheat a harmful food and says it differs greatly from wheat of past decades; he also says it stimulates appetite.[1] The plan is low-carbohydrate and grain-free. He has said a plant-based version using legumes, seeds and nuts is possible.[1]

The book sold strongly, while scientific and dietetic communities were largely critical. A 2012 analysis by Julie Jones said it confused correlation with causation and ignored contrary studies.[1] Harriet Hall described it as another low-carbohydrate plan that overlooks much evidence.[1]
A 2015 review in Annals of Nutrition and Metabolism discusses adverse effects of wheat gluten and the role of cereals in diets worldwide.[2]
No studies found of the Wheat Belly diet itself. A review of gluten's adverse effects exists for the broader topic.[2]

timeline.event: Wheat Belly published and becomes a bestseller.[1]
Journal of Cereal Science review assesses the book's claims.[1]
